steps: Leaves produce sugars during photosynthesis; these sugars are converted mainly into sucrose for transport.
Sucrose is actively loaded from leaf cells into the sieve tubes of the phloem, with the help of companion cells.
The increased sucrose concentration lowers the water potential in the sieve tubes, so water enters from the xylem by osmosis.
This entry of water raises the pressure in the sieve tubes at the source (the leaves).
The pressure pushes phloem sap towards sinks, such as roots, fruits and growing regions, where sugars are needed or stored.
Sucrose is unloaded at the sink; water may then leave the phloem and return to the xylem.
This movement of food from a source to a sink is called the pressure flow mechanism.
items.finalAnswer: Food moves through the phloem from sources to sinks because a pressure difference is produced by sugar loading and unloading.

steps: Plants lose extra water mainly by transpiration through the stomata of leaves.
Liquid water may also be removed as droplets through hydathodes at the margins or tips of leaves; this process is called guttation.
Excess salts and other wastes may be stored in leaves, bark or fruits, which are later shed.
Some plants also remove wastes in substances such as gums, resins and latex.
items.finalAnswer: Plants remove extra water by transpiration and guttation, and get rid of salts and other wastes by storing or secreting them and shedding waste-containing parts.

steps: Gaseous exchange in plants takes place mainly by diffusion through stomata in leaves and lenticels in stems.
During photosynthesis, carbon dioxide diffuses into the leaves and oxygen diffuses out through the stomata.
During respiration, oxygen diffuses into plant tissues and carbon dioxide diffuses out.
The direction of gaseous exchange depends on the plant’s activities and the concentration of gases inside and outside the plant.
items.finalAnswer: Plants exchange gases by diffusion, mainly through stomata in leaves and lenticels in stems.

steps: Plants do not have specialised excretory organs; wastes are removed or stored in different ways.
Gaseous wastes diffuse out through stomata in leaves and lenticels in stems.
Extra water is lost by transpiration and may also be removed by guttation through hydathodes.
Some wastes are stored in vacuoles or in leaves, bark and old xylem.
Wastes such as gums, resins and latex may be secreted.
Waste-containing leaves and bark are shed, removing the stored wastes from the plant.
items.finalAnswer: Plants excrete wastes by diffusion, water loss, secretion and storage in parts that are later shed.

steps: Hydrophytes live in water and generally have dilute cell sap because water is readily available.
Xerophytes live in dry habitats and have concentrated cell sap, which helps their cells absorb and retain water.
Halophytes grow in salty habitats and adjust osmotically by accumulating salts or other solutes in their cells.
These adjustments help plant cells maintain water balance in their particular habitats.
items.finalAnswer: Hydrophytes have dilute cell sap, xerophytes have concentrated cell sap, and halophytes adjust their cell solute concentration to live in salty conditions.

steps: Wind removes the moist layer of air that collects around the surface of leaves.
This maintains a steep difference in water-vapour concentration between the leaf and the surrounding air, so water vapour diffuses out faster.
Humid air already contains much water vapour, so the difference in water-vapour concentration between the leaf and the air is smaller.
Therefore, transpiration is generally faster on a windy day than on a humid day.
items.finalAnswer: Wind increases transpiration by removing moist air around leaves, while humid air reduces the water-vapour gradient and slows it.
